hotspots.topic: Air terminal placement and zone of protection
hotspots.whyItMatters: Strike-termination layout is the geometry-heavy centerpiece of lightning-protection design.
hotspots.cite: NFPA 780 — General Requirements chapter, Class I/II systems (confirm chapter number in your 2017 edition)
hotspots.trap: Spacing air terminals by a single rule-of-thumb distance without checking the class-dependent (Class I vs. Class II) spacing/height rule that actually governs.

hotspots.whyItMatters: The path from air terminal to ground, and bonding to other grounded building systems, is what prevents dangerous side-flash.
hotspots.cite: NFPA 780 — Down Conductors/Bonding section (confirm section number in your edition)
hotspots.trap: Routing a down conductor too close to metal ductwork or piping without the required bonding or separation distance, creating a side-flash path.

hotspots.topic: Grounding electrode requirements for lightning protection
hotspots.whyItMatters: LPS grounding electrodes have their own resistance/quantity rules, distinct from — but bonded to — the building's NEC Article 250 grounding electrode system.
hotspots.cite: NFPA 780 — Grounding chapter (confirm chapter number in your edition)
hotspots.trap: Assuming the building's NEC electrical grounding electrode automatically satisfies the LPS grounding requirement without the required bonding and verification.

hotspots.topic: Surge protection at the service entrance
hotspots.whyItMatters: Lightning-protection design pairs with surge protection to protect the electrical system, not just structural strike termination.
hotspots.cite: NFPA 780 — surge protection section (confirm section in your edition); cross-check NEC 230.67
hotspots.trap: Treating the structural lightning protection system as sufficient protection for sensitive electronics without a coordinated SPD strategy.
